--- title: "3D Population Density Mapping of Nepal" description: "A 3D population density map of Nepal built in R with rayshader and Kontur population data." image-alt: "3D population density map of Nepal with tall orange columns marking Kathmandu and other cities." subtitle: "Using Rayshader for Advanced Geospatial Visualization" author: - name: Pukar Bhandari email: pukar.bhandari@outlook.com image: "nepal_population_density.png" date: "2023-01-03" categories: [R, GIS, Data Science] prefer-html: true code-links: - text: Source of this post icon: github href: https://github.com/ar-puuk/ar-puuk.github.io/blob/master/posts/nepal-population-density/index.qmd - text: Project repository icon: github href: https://github.com/ar-puuk/Population-Density-Maps --- ## Project Overview This analysis demonstrates advanced geospatial visualization techniques using R's rayshader package to create a stunning 3D population density map of Nepal. The project showcases the integration of high-resolution population data with topographic visualization methods, resulting in an interactive and informative representation of demographic patterns across Nepal's diverse terrain. **Key Technologies**: R, rayshader, sf, stars, ragg, grid\ **Data Source**: Kontur Population Dataset (400m H3 hexagon resolution)\ **Projection**: ESRI:102306 (Nepal Nagarkot TM) ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"} ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-pipeline %%| fig-cap: "From population hexagons to the annotated 3D map." flowchart LR A["Kontur
hexagons"] --> B["Reproject
EPSG:6207"] B --> C["Rasterize
with stars"] C --> D["Height
matrix"] D --> E["3D scene
rayshader"] E --> F["Path-traced
render"] F --> G["Labels
with grid"] ``` ::: The steps are explained in @sec-raster for the raster, @sec-render for the 3D scene and @sec-annotate for the labels. ## Environment Setup ### Package Installation and Loading ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Package Installation (Run Once)"} # Core packages for geospatial analysis install.packages(c("here", "sf", "ggplot2", "stars")) # Visualization packages install.packages(c("rayshader", "MetBrewer", "colorspace", "rayrender")) # Annotation: PNG reading, anti-aliased PNG device, and font registration install.packages(c("png", "ragg", "systemfonts")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the packages"} library(here) library(sf) library(stars) library(rayshader) library(MetBrewer) library(colorspace) library(rayrender) # Annotation: PNG reading, anti-aliased PNG device, and font registration # (grid ships with base R) library(png) library(ragg) library(systemfonts) library(grid) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Configure 3D rendering options(rgl.useNULL = FALSE) project_crs <- "EPSG:6207" ``` ::: ## Data Acquisition and Loading ### Population Hexagon Data The analysis utilizes high-resolution population data from Kontur, provided in H3 hexagonal grid format at 400-meter resolution. This dataset offers superior granularity compared to traditional administrative boundary-based population estimates. ::: {.column-margin} [H3](https://h3geo.org/) is a hierarchical hexagonal grid. Hexagons are used because every neighbour is the same distance from the centre, which makes density maps smoother than square cells. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load population data (H3 hexagons at 400m resolution) nep_hex <- sf::st_read( paste0( "/vsigzip/", here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/data/kontur_population_NP_20220630.gpkg.gz") ) ) |> sf::st_transform(project_crs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `population' from data source `/vsigzip/D:/GitHub/ar-puuk.github.io/posts/nepal-population-density/data/kontur_population_NP_20220630.gpkg.gz' using driver `GPKG' Simple feature collection with 122809 features and 2 fields Geometry type: POLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 8911286 ymin: 3041698 xmax: 9818046 ymax: 3562066 Projected CRS: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load administrative boundaries nep_admin <- sf::st_read( paste0( "/vsigzip/", here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/data/kontur_boundaries_NP_20220407.gpkg.gz") ) ) |> sf::st_transform(project_crs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `sql_statement' from data source `/vsigzip/D:/GitHub/ar-puuk.github.io/posts/nepal-population-density/data/kontur_boundaries_NP_20220407.gpkg.gz' using driver `GPKG' Simple feature collection with 4902 features and 5 fields Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 80.05862 ymin: 26.34776 xmax: 88.20153 ymax: 30.44694 Geodetic CRS: WGS 84 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create unified Nepal boundary nepal_boundary <- nep_admin |> sf::st_geometry() |> sf::st_union() |> sf::st_sf() |> sf::st_make_valid() ``` ::: ::: callout-note **Data Sources**: - **Population Data**: [Kontur Population Dataset](https://data.humdata.org/dataset/kontur-population-nepal) - **Administrative Boundaries**: [Kontur Boundaries Dataset](https://data.humdata.org/dataset/kontur-boundaries-nepal) - **Coordinate Reference System**: EPSG:6207 for accurate representation of Nepal's geography ::: ## Data Processing and Visualization Setup ### Initial Data Exploration A quick map (@fig-exploration) confirms the hexagons line up with the national boundary before any 3D work starts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(nep_hex) + ggplot2::geom_sf(ggplot2::aes(fill = population), color = "gray66", linewidth = 0) + ggplot2::geom_sf(data = nepal_boundary, fill = NA, color = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + ggplot2::theme_minimal() + ggplot2::labs(title = "Nepal Population Distribution", fill = "Population") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Population in each 400 m hexagon, with the national boundary dashed.](index_files/figure-docx/fig-exploration-1.png){#fig-exploration fig-alt='Map of Nepal in hexagonal cells shaded by population. The cells with the most people cluster along the southern lowlands and around Kathmandu, and the dashed outline marks the national border.'} ::: ::: ### Raster Conversion and Matrix Preparation {#sec-raster} The conversion from vector hexagon data to raster format is essential for rayshader's 3D rendering capabilities. This process involves calculating optimal dimensions while preserving the geographic aspect ratio. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bbox <- sf::st_bbox(nepal_boundary) bottom_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |> # <1> sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs) bottom_right <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmax"]], bbox[["ymin"]])) |> sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs) top_left <- sf::st_point(c(bbox[["xmin"]], bbox[["ymax"]])) |> sf::st_sfc(crs = project_crs) width <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, bottom_right) # <2> height <- sf::st_distance(bottom_left, top_left) if(width > height) { # <3> w_ratio <- 1 h_ratio <- height / width } else { h_ratio <- 1 w_ratio <- width / height } size <- 1000 * 2.5 # <4> pop_raster <- stars::st_rasterize(nep_hex, # <5> nx = floor(size * w_ratio), ny = floor(size * h_ratio)) pop_matrix <- matrix(pop_raster$population, # <6> nrow = floor(size * w_ratio), ncol = floor(size * h_ratio)) ``` ::: 1. Three corners of the bounding box are enough to measure its width and height. 2. Distances come out in metres, because the CRS is projected. 3. Scale the longer side to 1 and the shorter side in proportion, so the map keeps its shape. 4. The longer side of the raster is 2,500 cells, a balance between detail and render time. 5. Burn the hexagons into a grid of cells, each holding that area's population. 6. Rayshader works on a plain matrix of heights, so the population grid becomes the heightmap. ## Color Scheme Development ### MetBrewer Color Palette Selection The visualization employs the "OKeeffe2" palette from MetBrewer, chosen for its warm earth tones that effectively represent population density while maintaining visual appeal and accessibility. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} color <- MetBrewer::met.brewer("OKeeffe2") # <1> texture <- grDevices::colorRampPalette(color, bias = 3)(256) # <2> colorspace::swatchplot(texture) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-docx/color-palette-1.png) ::: ::: 1. The palette's colours, from light sand to deep red. 2. Stretch it to 256 steps. `bias = 3` spends more of the range on the high values, so dense areas stand out against the sparse ones. ## 3D Visualization Rendering ### Interactive 3D Display {#sec-render} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rgl::close3d() # <1> pop_matrix |> rayshader::height_shade(texture = texture) |> # <2> rayshader::plot_3d( heightmap = pop_matrix, zscale = 250 / 2.5, # <3> solid = FALSE, shadowdepth = 0 ) rayshader::render_camera( # <4> theta = 0, phi = 30, zoom = 0.4, fov = 90 ) ``` ::: 1. Close any 3D window left open by an earlier run. 2. Colour each cell from the palette according to its population. 3. The vertical exaggeration: the smaller the number, the taller the peaks. 4. Look from the south (`theta = 0`), tilted 30 degrees down, with a wide field of view. ### High-Quality Rendering The final rendering process utilizes rayshader's advanced lighting system to create publication-ready visualizations with professional-grade quality and resolution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} outfile <- here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/plots/final_plot.png") # Render high-quality image with timing { start_time <- Sys.time() cat(crayon::cyan("Rendering started:", start_time), "\n") if(!file.exists(outfile)) { png::writePNG(matrix(1), target = outfile) # <1> } rayshader::render_highquality( # <2> filename = outfile, interactive = FALSE, lightdirection = 225, lightaltitude = c(20, 80), # <3> lightcolor = c(color[2], "white"), lightintensity = c(600, 100), width = 1980, height = 1080, samples = 300 # <4> ) end_time <- Sys.time() diff <- end_time - start_time cat(crayon::cyan("Rendering completed in:", diff), "\n") } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rendering started: 2026-11-13 09:03:31.056415 Rendering completed in: 9.15155640045802 ``` ::: ::: 1. Make sure the output file exists before the renderer writes to it. 2. A path-traced render: slow, but with soft shadows and realistic lighting. 3. Two lights, one low and warm and one high and white, shining from the south-west (225 degrees). 4. More samples smooth the noise of path tracing, at the cost of render time. ## Post-Processing and Annotation ### Geographic Labeling {#sec-annotate} The final step adds the title, city labels and attribution on top of the rendered image. Instead of {magick}, it uses base {grid} for layout and the {ragg} PNG device for anti-aliased text. Two font files in the `font/` folder are registered for the session with {systemfonts}, so nothing needs to be installed in Windows: Ananda Namaste for the title, and Jost Medium (a free Google Fonts typeface in the style of Futura) for everything else. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} systemfonts::register_font( # <1> "Ananda Namaste", plain = here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/font/Ananda Namaste 400.ttf") ) systemfonts::register_font( # <2> "Jost Medium", plain = here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/font/Jost-500.ttf") ) text_color <- colorspace::darken(color[7], .5) # <3> colorspace::swatchplot(text_color) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-docx/font-setup-1.png) ::: ::: 1. Register the bundled font for this session only, so nothing needs to be installed on the computer. 2. Jost (Google Fonts, OFL) stands in for Futura BT Medium, which is commercial. 3. The label colour is a darker shade of the palette, so it sits comfortably on the map. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load rendered image render <- png::readPNG( here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/plots/final_plot.png") ) img_h <- dim(render)[1] img_w <- dim(render)[2] add_label <- function(label, gravity, dx, dy, size, alpha = 0.8, # <1> family = "Jost Medium") { pos <- switch( # <2> gravity, northeast = list(x = img_w - dx, y = dy, h = 1, v = 1), east = list(x = img_w - dx, y = img_h / 2 + dy, h = 1, v = 0.5), west = list(x = dx, y = img_h / 2 + dy, h = 0, v = 0.5), center = list(x = img_w / 2 + dx, y = img_h / 2 + dy, h = 0.5, v = 0.5), southwest = list(x = dx, y = img_h - dy, h = 0, v = 0) ) grid::grid.text( # <3> label, x = grid::unit(pos$x, "native"), y = grid::unit(pos$y, "native"), hjust = pos$h, vjust = pos$v, gp = grid::gpar( col = grDevices::adjustcolor(text_color, alpha.f = alpha), fontsize = size, fontfamily = family ) ) } ``` ::: 1. Labels are placed ImageMagick-style, with a named edge and pixel offsets, because that is how the original version of this map was labelled. 2. The offsets move a label inward from the named edge. For `"center"`, positive x is right and positive y is down. 3. Draw the text with `grid`, so the anti-aliased `ragg` device handles the rendering. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ragg::agg_png( # <1> here::here("posts/nepal-population-density/nepal_population_density.png"), width = img_w, height = img_h, units = "px", res = 72 ) grid::grid.newpage() grid::grid.raster(render, width = 1, height = 1) grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(xscale = c(0, img_w), yscale = c(img_h, 0))) # <2> label_width <- function(label, size, family) { # <3> grid::convertWidth( grid::grobWidth(grid::textGrob( label, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = size, fontfamily = family) )), "native", valueOnly = TRUE ) } subtitle_size <- 36.5 subtitle_width <- label_width("POPULATION DENSITY MAP", subtitle_size, "Jost Medium") title_size <- 1.04 * 100 * subtitle_width / label_width("NEPAL", 100, "Ananda Namaste") # <4> add_label("NEPAL", "northeast", 50, 65, title_size, alpha = 1, family = "Ananda Namaste") add_label("POPULATION DENSITY MAP", "northeast", 50, 235, subtitle_size, alpha = 1) # Major urban centers add_label("Kathmandu", "center", 250, -50, 30) add_label("Pokhara", "center", -30, 35, 25) add_label("Biratnagar", "east", 125, 100, 28) # Regional centers add_label("Birgunj", "center", 130, 100, 25) add_label("Nepalgunj", "center", -450, 0, 24) add_label("Janakpur", "east", 500, 140, 22) # Additional urban areas add_label("Itahari", "east", 230, 150, 24) add_label("Surkhet", "center", -450, -75, 20) add_label("Tikapur", "west", 400, -125, 22) add_label("Dhangadhi", "west", 275, -135, 18) add_label("Bharatpur", "center", 60, 0, 20) add_label("Butwal", "center", -125, 5, 20) add_label("Ghorahi Tulsipur", "center", -350, -100, 22) # Attribution add_label( "Visualization by: Pukar Bhandari with Rayshader(@tylermorganwall) | Data: Kontur Population (Released 2022-06-30)", "southwest", 20, 20, 20, alpha = 0.6 ) invisible(grid::popViewport()) invisible(dev.off()) ``` ::: 1. At `res = 72` one point equals one pixel, so font sizes match the image's pixel grid. 2. Native units with y running top-down, so the pixel offsets in `add_label()` line up. 3. Measures how wide a piece of text will be, so the title can be sized to match the subtitle. 4. "NEPAL" is scaled so its width matches the subtitle's. Ananda Namaste has side bearings and an overhanging top bar on the "n", so the width is nudged up by 4% to line the stem of the "n" up with the "P". ![Population density of Nepal as a 3D map: tall orange columns mark Kathmandu and the cities of the southern lowlands.](nepal_population_density.png){#fig-final .lightbox fig-alt="3D population density map of Nepal. Tall orange and red columns rise from the southern lowlands and the Kathmandu valley, with low dark ground across the Himalaya. City names and the title NEPAL are printed on the map."} @fig-final is the finished map. Click it to enlarge. ## Technical Methodology ### Spatial Data Processing Pipeline 1. **Data Transformation**: Vector hexagon data converted to standardized coordinate reference system (Nepal Nagarkot TM - ESRI:102306) 2. **Rasterization**: Optimal grid resolution calculated to balance detail with computational efficiency (@sec-raster) 3. **Matrix Conversion**: Raster data transformed into height matrix for 3D rendering 4. **Texture Mapping**: Population values mapped to color gradients using perceptually uniform color spaces ### Rendering Specifications - **Resolution**: 1980×1080 pixels for high-definition output - **Sampling**: 300 samples for anti-aliasing and smooth gradients - **Lighting**: Dual-source lighting system (directional + ambient) - **Z-Scale**: Optimized vertical exaggeration (250/2.5) for clear population peaks ## Results and Applications This methodology produces publication-quality 3D population density visualizations suitable for: - **Urban Planning**: Identifying population clusters and growth patterns - **Infrastructure Development**: Targeting high-density areas for transportation networks - **Emergency Response**: Understanding population distribution for resource allocation - **Academic Research**: Visual communication of demographic data ## Conclusion This workflow demonstrates the power of combining modern R packages for geospatial analysis with advanced 3D visualization techniques. The resulting maps provide intuitive understanding of Nepal's population distribution patterns, highlighting the concentration of people in the Terai region and major urban centers while showcasing the relatively sparse population in mountainous areas. The methodology is transferable to other geographic contexts and can be adapted for various demographic or infrastructure planning applications in transportation and urban development projects. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ *Want to contribute or suggest improvements?
